threads.thread_goal: Align on current customer journey and main pain points across channels.

messages.text: Hi team, let's kick off by mapping how customers experience us right now across store, contact centre, and field sales. I'd like each of you to share one or two key pain points you see in your channel—what frustrates customers most? We'll use this to shape T1 and feed into A5 later. Please share by EOD tomorrow.

Good timing. In field sales, I see customers get confused about follow-up timelines. We visit, make a proposal, but then there's no clear next step documented. Customers call the contact centre asking 'what happened to my quote?' and we have no record. That's a big gap.

From my side, similar issue. Customers don't know what to expect after a visit. Also, when we hand off to the store team for delivery or follow-up, there's no shared understanding of what was promised. Store staff sometimes contradict what we said.

In-store, customers complain about inconsistent product info. One day a shelf is well-stocked and clean, next day it's messy. Also, when we get a complaint, we don't know if the contact centre already handled it or if it's new. No visibility across channels.

That's exactly what I'm hearing from contact centre calls too. Customers call in frustrated because they've already complained in-store, or they don't know who to contact. We're also getting repeat questions because there's no standard way to document what was discussed.

From the store floor, I'd add: customers don't get consistent greetings or help. Some staff jump in immediately, others ignore them. And when there's a refund or complaint, we handle it differently depending on who's working. No standard approach.
I see the same. Also, when we capture feedback from customers, it's scattered—some notes in a till receipt, some in a notebook, nothing consistent. Hard to spot trends or escalate issues properly.

Right. So I'm hearing four main themes: (1) lack of follow-up clarity between field and store, (2) inconsistent customer interactions and tone, (3) no shared complaint/feedback log, (4) refund and escalation rules vary by person. Does that capture it?
Yes, that's solid. I'd say the follow-up clarity is the biggest one for us in field sales. If we can nail that, customers will feel less abandoned.
Agreed. And the consistent interactions piece—if we all greet the same way and ask the same questions, customers will feel more confident. That's doable.
The feedback log is critical too. Right now we lose so much insight. If we had a simple way to log issues, we could spot patterns and fix things faster.

Perfect. So let me propose: we prioritise these four pain points as the core focus for the playbook. We'll design T1 to map the journey with these in mind, and we'll make sure A5 (the feedback log) is simple enough to use daily. Does everyone agree to focus on these four?
Yes, makes sense. I'll start sketching out the journey map from the field sales angle. Should have something rough by tomorrow afternoon.
Agreed. I can help with the feedback log structure once we have the journey mapped. Want to make sure we capture the right data points.

Great. So D1 is locked: we're prioritising follow-up clarity, consistent interactions, shared feedback log, and standardised refund/escalation rules. Now, for D2, I need us to agree on a simple journey diagram. I'll draft one based on what we've discussed and post it tomorrow. We'll review and sign off by end of week. Sound good?
Yes, let's do it. I'll be ready to review and give feedback on the store side of the journey.
I'll review from the account management perspective. Looking forward to seeing how the touchpoints connect.

Perfect. I'll have the draft journey diagram and a summary of T1 findings ready by tomorrow EOD. Everyone review and we'll lock D2 by Friday. This sets us up nicely for the playbook outline in the next thread.

threads.thread_goal: Define the structure and core behaviours of the unified playbook.

messages.text: Alright, now that we've mapped the journey and agreed on pain points, let's build the playbook structure. I've drafted an outline for A1 based on our four priorities. The idea is to have sections for store, contact centre, and field sales, with a shared 'core behaviours' section at the top. Here's the outline: (1) Core Behaviours—Greeting, Needs Analysis, Closing; (2) Store Channel—Merchandising, Cleanliness, Refunds; (3) Contact Centre—Call Flow, Escalation, Feedback Capture; (4) Field Sales—Visit Script, Follow-Up, Account Handoff. Thoughts?

Good structure. For field sales, I'd add a section on 'Handoff to Store' so we're clear on what info we pass and how. Also, the follow-up template needs to be linked to the feedback log so we don't lose track of commitments.

I like it. For store, I'd emphasise that the core behaviours—especially the greeting and needs analysis—should be the same whether it's a walk-in or a follow-up from field sales. That consistency is what customers want.

Exactly. So the core behaviours are the glue. Let me refine: Greeting (warm, open-ended question), Needs Analysis (listen, ask clarifying questions), Closing (confirm next steps, document). Does that work for all channels?

Yes, that's clear. But I need to flag: in busy peak hours, staff might rush the needs analysis. We need to make sure the playbook says it's okay to keep it brief if the customer is in a hurry. Otherwise, people will ignore it.
Good point. I'll add a note: 'Adapt to the customer's pace. If they're in a rush, keep it to one or two questions.' That way it's flexible but still structured.
I'm concerned about the 'Closing' step. In field sales, we often need to follow up later with a quote or proposal. How do we document that in the playbook without making it too complex?

That's where T5 comes in—the field sales visit script and follow-up template. We'll have a simple one-page template that captures the visit summary and next steps. The playbook will reference it, but won't duplicate it. Does that help?
Yes, that works. And the follow-up template should feed into A5 so the contact centre and store know what was promised. That closes the loop.

Exactly. So let me lock D3: we approve the playbook structure as I outlined—Core Behaviours, Store, Contact Centre, Field Sales—with the flexibility note for peak hours and the handoff section for field sales. Everyone good?
Yes, I'm in. Now, for D4, what are the 3–5 core behaviours we want to be common across all channels? I think we've identified Greeting, Needs Analysis, and Closing. Should we add anything else?

Good question. I'd add 'Document and Escalate'—meaning, after the interaction, we log what happened and flag any issues. That's critical for the feedback loop. So: Greeting, Needs Analysis, Closing, Document, Escalate. That's five. Does that cover it?
I'd say that's solid. But 'Document' might be tricky for busy staff. Can we make it simple—like, just note the issue on the feedback sheet if there's a problem?

Yes, that's the idea. 'Document' means: if there's a complaint, refund, or special request, jot it on A5. If it's routine, no need. We'll clarify that in the playbook and in T4 for contact centre and T5 for field sales.

Perfect. So D4 is locked: Greeting, Needs Analysis, Closing, Document, Escalate. These five behaviours are common across store, contact centre, and field sales. Now we need to flesh out T4 and T5 to show how each channel applies these.

Right. I'll draft T4 (contact centre call flow) and T5 (field sales script) by tomorrow. I'll also update A1 with the five core behaviours and the channel-specific sections. Everyone review by Friday and we'll lock the playbook structure. Sound good?

threads.thread_goal: Agree on in-store checklist, refunds policy, and job aids content.

messages.text: Hi all, I've drafted the in-store merchandising and cleanliness checklist for A2. It covers product displays, stock levels, and cleanliness zones. The idea is staff can run through it in under 5 minutes at the start of each shift. Here's the draft: (1) Check displays are tidy and signage is clear; (2) Restock any empty shelves; (3) Sweep and wipe down high-touch areas; (4) Check for any damaged products. Simple, right? I'd like feedback from the store side and from field sales on whether this aligns with what customers see.

Good start. I'd add one more: check that product info cards are in place and accurate. Customers get frustrated when they can't find prices or details. Also, the checklist should note that if something is broken or missing, we flag it for the manager immediately.

Good points. I'll add those. So the checklist becomes: (1) Displays tidy, signage clear, product info cards in place; (2) Restock empty shelves; (3) Sweep and wipe high-touch areas; (4) Check for damaged products and flag to manager; (5) Verify prices are correct. Still under 5 minutes?

From field sales perspective, when we bring customers in for a follow-up visit or demo, the store environment matters a lot. If it's messy, customers lose confidence. This checklist will help. One thing: can you add a note about greeting customers who come in? That ties back to the core behaviours.

Good idea. I'll add a note at the top: 'Before starting the checklist, greet any customers in the store and offer help.' That way the checklist is part of the daily routine, not separate from customer service.
This looks solid. Now, while we're on the store side, we also need to lock down the refunds and complaints policy. That's T6. I know 200631 is working on that. Can you share a draft?

I've got a draft for A6. The idea is to have clear rules so every staff member handles refunds and complaints the same way. Here's the outline: (1) Refunds under £50—staff can approve on the spot; (2) Refunds £50–£200—need manager approval; (3) Refunds over £200—escalate to contact centre; (4) Complaints—log on A5 and escalate if customer is upset. Does that make sense?

That's clear. But I want to make sure the contact centre can apply the same rules. Can you add a note that says 'Contact centre follows the same thresholds, and can approve refunds up to £200 without store approval'? That way we're aligned.

Yes, I'll add that. Also, I want to include a few examples of typical complaints—like 'product arrived damaged' or 'customer changed their mind'—so staff know how to categorise them. That way we're consistent.
From field sales, I'd add one more scenario: what if a customer says 'I was promised a discount by the account manager'? How do we verify that and handle it?

Good catch. I'll add: 'If customer claims a discount was promised, ask for the account manager's name and check the follow-up template (T5). If verified, honour it. If not verified, escalate to manager.' That way we protect both the customer and the business.

Perfect. So D5: we sign off on the final version of A2 (the checklist) with the greeting note and the five-step process. And D6: we approve A6 (refunds and complaints policy) with the thresholds, examples, and the discount verification rule. Everyone agree?
Yes, I'm happy with A2. One last thing: we also need to create the job aids (A7). Should we do that now or wait for the full playbook to be done?

Good question. Let's do it now. T8 is to create job aids that summarise the 3–5 key behaviours per channel. I'll draft one for contact centre, and I'd like 45990 to draft one for store and 49060 to draft one for field sales. These should be one-page cards that staff can keep at their desk or in their pocket. Can you do that by Friday?
Yes, I can do that. I'll focus on the store job aid: greeting, needs analysis, closing, document, escalate—with examples for each. Should be quick.
I'll draft the field sales job aid. I'll include the visit script outline and the follow-up template reference. Should be straightforward.

Great. So to recap: D5 and D6 are locked. A2 and A6 are approved. Now we're moving to A7 (job aids) with drafts due Friday. Once we have those, we'll review them in the next thread along with the training plan. Sound good?

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot, training sessions, and feedback collection approach.

messages.text: Alright, we're in the home stretch. We've got the playbook structure, the checklist, the refunds policy, and the job aids. Now we need to plan the pilot and training. Here's my proposal for D7: we run a two-week pilot with one store location and two account managers. The store will test A2, A6, and A7. The account managers will test T5 and the follow-up process. The contact centre (that's us) will test T4 and A3. Does that scope make sense?
I can do the pilot with one of my accounts. But I need to know: will the store staff be trained before we start, or do we train them as part of the pilot?

Good question. I think we should do a quick training session before the pilot starts. That's T9. We'll run a 1-hour session for the store staff and a 1-hour session for the account managers. That leaves 1 hour for contact centre training. Everyone gets 2 hours total, which fits the constraint.
One hour for store training might be tight. We need to cover the checklist, the refunds policy, the job aid, and the core behaviours. Can we do 1.5 hours?

The constraint is 2 hours total per worker. If we do 1.5 for store, that leaves 0.5 for contact centre, which is too short. Let me propose: 1 hour for store (focus on checklist and core behaviours), 0.75 for account managers (focus on visit script and follow-up), 0.25 for contact centre (we can do a quick huddle). That's 2 hours total. Does that work?
I think that's tight for contact centre. We need to understand the call flow and escalation rules. Can we do the training in two sessions—one before the pilot and one after the first week?

That's a good idea. Let me revise: we do a 1-hour pre-pilot training for store and account managers. Then, during the pilot, we do a 0.5-hour check-in for contact centre after the first week. That way we can adjust based on what we're seeing. Does that fit the 2-hour constraint?
Yes, that works for me. So we do a 1-hour training before the pilot, then a 0.5-hour check-in mid-pilot, then a 0.5-hour debrief after. That's 2 hours total and gives us time to adjust.

Perfect. So D8 part one: we agree on the training schedule—1 hour pre-pilot, 0.5 hour mid-pilot check-in, 0.5 hour post-pilot debrief. Now, for the feedback collection during the pilot, we'll use A5 (the feedback log). I want to make sure we're capturing the right data. T7 is to create the feedback sheet. 24573, can you draft that?
Yes, I can do that. I'll create a simple sheet with columns for date, channel, issue type, customer comment, and action taken. Should be usable on paper and in a spreadsheet.
Good. And I want to add one more column: 'Playbook helped?' Yes or No. That way we can see if the playbook is actually making a difference. Can you add that?
Yes, I'll add that. So the sheet will have: date, channel, issue type, customer comment, action taken, playbook helped? That should give us good insight.

Perfect. Now, for the weekly reporting routine, that's T10. I'll draft a simple template that pulls data from A5 and shows trends. We'll review it with the pilot group and adjust if needed. Does that work?
Yes. And I want to make sure we're tracking follow-up completion rates from field sales. That's a key metric for us. Can we add that to the weekly report?

Absolutely. So the weekly report will include: (1) Total issues logged, (2) Issues by type, (3) Playbook helped? Yes/No ratio, (4) Follow-up completion rate (field sales), (5) Refund approvals and escalations. That's five metrics. Sound good?
That's solid. But who's responsible for updating the weekly report? Is it the store, the account managers, or the contact centre?

Good question. I'll assign it: store staff logs issues on A5 daily, account managers log follow-ups daily, contact centre (me) compiles the weekly report every Friday. That way it's clear who does what.

So D8 part two: we agree on the weekly reporting routine—store logs daily, account managers log daily, contact centre compiles Friday. Now, let's lock the pilot timeline. I propose: training next Monday, pilot runs for two weeks (Monday to Friday of week two), mid-pilot check-in on Wednesday of week one, debrief on Friday of week two. Then we have the weekend to adjust and roll out the following Monday. Does that work?
That timeline works for me. I'll make sure my pilot account is ready by Monday.
Yes, I can have the store ready. I'll make sure the checklist is printed and the job aids are posted.

Great. So D7 is locked: one store, two account managers, contact centre pilot. And D8 is locked: training schedule and weekly reporting routine. Now, T11 is to validate the playbook with the pilot group and collect feedback. T12 is to finalise the playbook after the pilot. I'll own both of those. By the end of week two, we'll have a final playbook ready for rollout. Sound good?
Perfect. This is a solid plan. I'm confident we can pull this off in the timeline.

Excellent. Let me summarise the next steps: 24573 drafts A5 by tomorrow, I draft T10 by tomorrow, 45990 and 49060 finalise the job aids by Friday, we do training next Monday, pilot runs for two weeks, and we debrief and finalise by end of week two. Everyone clear on their tasks?
